newsitem.title: USA: Former Lake aides quizzed on eve of CIA hearings.
newsitem.headline: Former Lake aides quizzed on eve of CIA hearings.

text.p: Senate committee staff on Monday questioned current and former National Security Council aides on the eve of politically tense confirmation hearings for Anthony Lake to be CIA director.

Staff members of the Senate Intelligence Committee said they were taking unsworn testimony from the Asia specialists who worked for Lake when he was national security adviser during President Bill Clinton's first term.

At issue, among other things, is what Lake and his White House staff knew about alleged efforts by China and possibly other foreign governments to pump laundered funds into political races to illegally influence U.S. foreign policy.

The growing stir over improper foreign campaign contributions was only one of many political minefields facing Lake during a tentatively scheduled six days of hearings that start on Tuesday afternoon.
Senate Minority leader Thomas Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, said Monday he was "very displeased" with Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Shelby's handling so far of the Lake nomination.
"I think that Senator Shelby (an Alabama Republican) has chosen to be very political on this nomination, and I think it's been disingenuous in some cases," he told reporters.
Lake appears to have enough backing in the 19-member intelligence panel to win its approval barring any bombshell disclosures.

Two senior Republican members, Sens. Richard Lugar of Indiana and John Chafee of Rhode Island, have said they are inclined to vote in favour. With the likely support of the nine Democratic members, that would be enough to send the nomination to the floor of the Senate.
Shelby said on Sunday that Lake might still run into a "firestorm" on the Senate floor even if his nomination clears the committee.
Shelby said he was still not satisfied with a White House-proposed compromise on his demand for fuller access to Lake's complete FBI background file. "We're still negotiating," he said.

Clinton urged the Senate on Monday to confirm Lake as quickly as possible. "He believes Mr. Lake is uniquely qualified for this important post and wants his national security team in place," a White House statement said.
One focus of the hearings will be alleged failings of Clinton's foreign policies in hot spots like Bosnia, Somalia and Haiti.

Senators also were expected to ask Lake about an alleged White House coverup of Chinese missile sales to Pakistan. Another issue will be a decision to keep Congress, especially the intelligence panels, in the dark about tacit U.S. support of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994.
White House aides have suggested that Shelby hopes to use the hearings to embarrass Clinton and make a partisan political splash, a charge he denied.

In a recent interview, Shelby cited a need to get the right person to preside over the Central Intelligence Agency and its 12 sister intelligence outfits that together account for up to $30 billion in annual U.S. spending. Lake would be Clinton's third CIA chief and the fifth in six years.

The current and former National Security Council aides being interviewed on Monday were Sandra Kristoff, head of the Asia directorate; Robert Suettinger, a China expert; Melanie Darby, a former staff member, and Stanley Roth, who was in charge of Asia policy from March 1994 until Jan. 1, 1996.

According to documents released by the White House, Kristoff met at least twice with Pauline Kanchanalak, a Thai businesswoman and lobbyist whose $253,000 in now-returned contributions to the Democratic party are the subject of a criminal investigation.
